comparator.name: Liberal Arts and Sciences
comparator.route: Interdisciplinary Social Sciences; Transformations to Sustainability
comparator.sourceNotes: Fresh 31 October 2026 inspection of the official 2026-entry tables establishes four majors and three themes. One coherent 180-EC pathway is instantiated: common Year 1 36 + ISS major 24; common Year 2 12 + ISS major 30 + sustainability theme 18; Year 3 mobility 30 + Senior Seminar 6 + theme capstone 12 + major thesis 12. Nine named ISS courses include the first two listed major electives, Statistics 2 and Sociological Themes. The theme has two named required courses and one genuine approved 6-EC elective. Mobility retains five approved options. GROW is zero-credit. Dedicated major identity controls BSc status over the generic BA table heading; copied ISS headings on other major pages do not override their named programmes and course content.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Interdisciplinary analysis of complex social issues across philosophy, law, sociology, psychology, neuroscience, politics and economics
Social structures, inequality, migration, diversity, polarisation and relationships between individuals and communities
Law, politics, culture, democracy, justice, power and institutions
Brain, behaviour, emotion, cognition, resilience and well-being
Interdisciplinary qualitative and quantitative research applied to real-world social challenges
adjacent: Transformations to sustainability and environmental governance
Technology and society, including algorithmic thinking, AI ethics and digital culture
questions: Structured major and societal-theme choices that let students combine depth with interdisciplinary breadth
Career and further-study trajectories in policy, research, public service, neuroscience, sustainability and consultancy

trace: Mandatory Year-1 academic writing, scholarly source evaluation, research questions and community-engaged reflection support interdisciplinary learning; not a substitute for a thesis.
Microeconomic markets, strategic choice and short-run macroeconomic models supply the economic lens on societal and organisational questions.
Public goods, externalities, taxation, redistribution, welfare and social insurance provide substantive economic analysis of inequality and collective policy choices.
Measurement, sampling, design, estimation, hypothesis testing and regression support empirical social/behavioural inquiry through an actual data-collection project.

Emotion regulation, belonging, identity safety and inclusive leadership connect minority experiences and social interaction with a supervised quantitative inclusion survey; not general wellbeing or all diversity policy.
Motivation, teams, power, organisational structure/culture and evidence synthesis provide sustained organisational-behaviour inquiry, not generic leadership alone.
Fairness, privacy, responsibility, agency and psychological human-AI interaction provide substantive digital-ethics inquiry, not programming.
R-based cleaning, joining, visualization and textual/spatial data analysis support research; no neuroscience-specific dataset or statistical-inference sequence is assumed.
Python control flow, functions, recursion, data collections, testing and debugging provide actual algorithmic problem-solving and computational tools.
Institutions, actors, justice and systemic/technological responses support sustainability transformation; stakeholder inquiry and policy advice give defined applied governance work.
Climate mechanisms, impacts, justice, governance and mitigation/adaptation connect physical change to societal responses and communication.
Legal traditions, public/private law and socio-legal justice questions provide foundational legal/normative inquiry with case reasoning and a research proposal.
Political, economic and cultural change since 1815 contextualises democracy, nationalism, imperialism and social transformation; narrower in period than all European history.
Intersectional North American gender histories, primary sources, queer lives and activism examine how institutions and cultural narratives shape identity and resistance.
Indigenous social/cultural histories, institutional violence and contemporary resurgence provide a distinct historical/cultural account of power and collective agency.

Historical questions, critical source engagement, interdisciplinary thinking and a substantial research paper develop historical inquiry. No archived project, geographic case or detailed period content is assumed beyond the current title and description.
Human-rights law, institutions, landmark cases and philosophical critiques examine rights, dignity, democracy and contested universality.
Criminal liability, punishment, criminalization and justice are tested through legal advice, oral argument and a criminological research proposal.
International legal sources, responsibility, force, human rights, self-determination and treaty politics connect law with public power and global institutions.
Constitutional structures, rights, judicial review and administrative fairness are studied through concrete cross-system comparison and legal application.
Comparative property, tort and contract law examines private rights, obligations, policy pressures and negotiated remedies.
EU institutions, supremacy, judicial remedies, citizenship and free movement provide substantive regional legal-order inquiry with digital/green applications.
Knowledge, ethics, consciousness, freedom and identity introduce critical philosophical arguments relevant to social, legal and mind questions.
Historical and contemporary ethical theories, goodness and moral argument supply a normative lens on societal choices, without claiming the complete interdisciplinary Evil subject.
Identity, consciousness, mind-body theories, neuropsychological cases and machine consciousness provide a philosophical counterpart to empirical cognition.
Philosophical accounts of emotion, knowledge, decision-making and political anger connect conceptual inquiry with emotional/social experience.
Agency, moral responsibility, determinism, luck, time and selfhood add a defined philosophical inquiry into action; not knowledge-and-power equivalence.
Comparison of democracy, institutions, parties, polarization and participation uses democracy measurement and a theory-guided empirical memo.
Competing international-relations theories, conflict, colonial relationships and climate politics support geopolitical analysis and researched multilateral negotiation.
EU institutions, representation and policymaking combine with empirical analysis of parliamentary amendments, ideology and possible interest-group influence.
Inequality, identity, colonial legacies, humanitarian law and peacebuilding integrate legal/social/political inquiry through a research dossier and policy brief.
Solidarity, identity, stratification, migration and inequality ground sociological analysis of social problems through theories and scholarly evidence.
Qualitative research design, ethics, reflexivity, interviews, ethnography, coding and interpretation implement an actual team inquiry into social experience.
Modern and contemporary sociological theories, Black feminist and decolonial perspectives support theoretically grounded interpretation of social phenomena.
Social movements and environmental justice are examined through Environmental Justice Atlas cases, feminism, anti-colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding.
Civil society, trust, solidarity, public spheres and decolonial theory frame a research project on a civil organisation, movement or initiative.
Comparative neuroanatomy, physiology, neural regulation, sleep and mood provide substantive biological explanations of behaviour.
Neural mechanisms of perception and goal-directed action are examined through cognitive-neuroscience and neuropsychological methods.
Attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control and consciousness are studied through neural function, an attention experiment and a designed research proposal.
Language acquisition, production, comprehension and impairments connect neuroscience, psychology and experimental approaches to linguistic capacity.
Neural signalling, anatomy, development and psychological processes introduce brain-behaviour relationships and interdisciplinary research-article analysis.
Social influence, self, groups, prejudice and prosocial behaviour explain individual-collective interaction; the final project designs rather than conducts empirical research.
Experimental design and multivariable statistical models support health/behavioural research, with assumption checks, model interpretation and data-analysis reporting.
Biopsychosocial psychopathology, diagnostic cases and explicit literature searching/appraisal deepen mental-health inquiry; no professional clinical qualification is claimed.
Health inequalities, stress, prevention, chronic illness and clinical-health formulation connect biological, psychological and social influences on health.
Psychological assessment, measurement quality, clinical interviews and psychotherapeutic approaches provide introductory diagnostic/clinical study and a case report.
Systematic review, effect sizes, fixed/random effects, heterogeneity and publication bias support quantitative evidence synthesis through a small group meta-analysis, not an independent thesis.
Physical, cognitive, emotional and social development across the lifespan connects theory with cases, interventions and a life-story interview.

Youth radicalization, protective factors and inclusive school climates connect psychology, sociology and civic education through research-based teacher/youth materials; not a general happiness course.
Public speaking, debating and storytelling are applied in reciprocal primary-school teaching and civic confidence; this is not a sustainability-governance capstone.
Persuasion, framing and ethical communication are applied with local climate partners to sustainable/circular lifestyles, supporting a defined societal-transformation question.
Close literary reading, form, narrative and critical sources supply tools to interpret cultural meaning and contested representations.
Moving-image form, film history, feminist/postcolonial interpretation and digital representation provide substantive cultural/media analysis.
American media history, storytelling, power, Indigenous self-representation and disability examine dominant cultural narratives and alternative futures.

alternatives.label: Society, organisations & sustainable public challenges
alternatives.concept: Sociology, organisational behaviour and economics connect with comparative politics, law, ethics and social psychology to examine inequality, communities and public choices. Qualitative and quantitative research, environmental justice, sustainability governance, climate science and digital inquiry support analysis of societal transformation.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum gives sustained weight to society, organisations, economic/public choices and sustainability, with research and interdisciplinary breadth. It materially responds to the selected ISS/sustainability pathway without claiming every Tilburg requirement.
progression: All current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked against the current workbook; Year-1 PPD retained. Statistics, economics, data and mathematical foundations considered as advisory preferences, not extra hard prerequisites.

alternatives.label: Cognitive neuroscience, behaviour & society
alternatives.concept: Brain and behaviour, neurobiology, higher cognitive functions, perception, language and psychological development form a sustained neuroscience and psychology inquiry. Experimental statistics, evidence synthesis and data work connect this inquiry to clinical, social and philosophical questions.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has a sequenced brain-and-behaviour, psychology, cognitive-neuroscience and research core while retaining social-science and philosophical breadth.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest match, this route replaces most law, public-policy and sustainability coursework with a sustained cognitive-neuroscience and psychology sequence including neurobiology, perception, higher-order functions, psycholinguistics and advanced behavioural research.
progression: All current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked against the current workbook; Year-1 PPD retained. Statistics, economics, data and mathematical foundations considered as advisory preferences, not extra hard prerequisites.

alternatives.label: Law, politics & contested culture
alternatives.concept: Public, constitutional, international, private and European law connect with democracy, international relations and peace/conflict. Historical inquiry, philosophy, rhetoric, literature and media examine how rights, power and cultural meanings are constructed and contested.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines a substantial law and politics sequence with philosophy, history, rhetoric, literature and media, so the label captures both institutional and cultural interpretation.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the other alternatives, this route replaces most psychology, neuroscience and sustainability coursework with public, international, constitutional, criminal, private and EU law plus political theory, history and cultural analysis.
progression: All current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked against the current workbook; Year-1 PPD retained. Statistics, economics, data and mathematical foundations considered as advisory preferences, not extra hard prerequisites.

blocks: Estimation, hypothesis tests and introductory regression provide foundational statistical inference and research design.
Qualitative design, reflexivity, interviews, coding and interpretation provide an important defined methodological part; the external introduction spans wider methods.
Neural anatomy/signalling and psychological behaviour provide direct introductory brain/behaviour study.

Social influence, group processes, prejudice and prosocial behaviour provide an identifiable psychological part of individual-collective relations, without covering all interdisciplinary social science.
Multivariable models, comparisons, assumptions and statistical reporting provide a substantive continuation, framed in health/behavioural research.
Microeconomic markets/choice and macroeconomic output, unemployment and inflation supply a substantial business/economic foundation, without a full changing-world business survey.
Redistribution, taxation, social insurance, welfare and efficiency/equity directly address an economic-policy part of socio-economic inequality.
Individual, team and organisational behaviour, motivation, power, structure and culture directly address people and organisations.
Legal institutions, public/private law, justice and social change address the legal/socio-legal part of the introductory law-politics-culture subject.
Sociological theories, stratification, identity, migration and inequality directly address introductory sociology.
Modern/contemporary sociological theories applied to social phenomena provide direct thematic sociological inquiry.
Civil society, trust, solidarity, public spheres and decolonial perspectives provide substantive community/collective-life inquiry; this is a theoretically focused partial relationship.
Political, economic and cultural history since 1815 provides an important modern-period relationship; the external European and religious scope is wider.
Human-AI agency, relationships, development, privacy and ethical implications supply a defined part of being human amid digital technology; wider digital culture remains broader.
Computational problem-solving, control flow, recursion, testing and Python programs provide actual algorithmic thinking.
Institutional, stakeholder and systemic/technological responses, policy feasibility and governance advice directly address sustainability transformation pathways.
Environmental justice, feminism, anti-colonialism, degrowth and movement case analysis supply substantive critical sustainability perspectives.
Other common requirements, research and genuine choice
Rhetoric, public law and democracy appear across separate courses; no one selected course establishes the integrated required subject.
Social psychology, health and youth prevention are specific subjects, not an independent counterpart to the full resilience, happiness and well-being course.
Ethical theory, criminal justice and conflict provide relevant lenses but do not establish the integrated Evil subject as a course purpose.
Philosophical and political inquiry alone does not establish the integrated knowledge/power requirement.
Preserve this genuine approved within-theme elective without inventing a selected subject.
Preserve genuine 30-EC approved mobility/minor choice without assigning a UCR-fit subject.
General methods or advanced coursework do not by themselves establish the required Senior Seminar.

Governance advice and climate communication support transformation but do not establish the required 12-EC Sustainability Think Tank and Governance capstone; governance has its stronger taught-course placement.
A group meta-analysis, methods course or historical paper does not establish the required independent major thesis; optional UCR research remains additional and unscheduled.

selection.assessment: The strongest closest response addresses the selected ISS/sustainability route through sustained social, organisational, economic, research and transformation study. Cognitive Neuroscience and Behavior and Law, Politics, and Culture then pass sequential evidence, coherence, substantive distinctness and feasibility gates. The current fourth major Design and Technology is explicitly considered after these three accepted curricula and excluded only at the three-alternative maximum; no no-match is inferred. All three societal-theme interests have substantive support within the closest public, digital and sustainability inquiry, while the comparator itself follows only the selected theme.

routeSelection.route: Interdisciplinary Social Sciences; Transformations to Sustainability
routeSelection.basis: No general/default route is advertised. Interdisciplinary Social Sciences is selected as the broadest social-science route, spanning sociology, economics, business, law and philosophy plus qualitative/quantitative inquiry, rather than the more focused brain, law/culture or design/technology majors. Themes are equally specialised; published order breaks the tie in favour of Transformations to Sustainability. The first two listed major electives, Statistics 2 and Sociological Themes, preserve broad methods and disciplinary inquiry. These choices are independent of UCR fit. The third approved theme elective and mobility window remain genuine choice.

notes.text: The Tilburg comparison follows Interdisciplinary Social Sciences with Transformations to Sustainability. Its named major requirements, required theme courses and theme-specific capstone differ from UCR’s three interdisciplinary approaches. The remaining approved theme elective and mobility window retain genuine choice. Shared rows indicate partial subject relationships; the required major thesis remains distinct from optional UCR research.

audience.programmeDescription: Liberal Arts and Sciences at Tilburg combines an interdisciplinary core with one of four majors and one of three societal themes. The selected pathway studies people, communities, organisations, inequality and digital life through Interdisciplinary Social Sciences, alongside Transformations to Sustainability. It leads to a Bachelor of Science.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR approaches these interests through society, organisations and sustainable public challenges; cognition and behaviour; or law, politics and contested culture. Each combines substantive disciplinary inquiry with research and broader perspectives. The comparison follows one defined Tilburg pathway, while the two related UCR directions also draw on its other established majors. Shared rows show partial subject relationships. Tilburg’s integrated core subjects, Senior Seminar, theme capstone and required thesis remain meaningful differences.

curriculum.routeLabel: Interdisciplinary Social Sciences; Transformations to Sustainability
curriculum.limitation: The 180-EC pathway includes Statistics 2 and Sociological Themes as its two major electives, two named required sustainability courses, a further approved 6-EC theme elective, 30 EC of approved mobility/minor choice, and a 12-EC major thesis. GROW activities carry no credits.

componentNotes.y2-theme-elective: One approved 6-EC elective within Transformations to Sustainability; the published overview leaves the specific selection open.
componentNotes.y3-mobility: Choose one approved 30-EC option: exchange, Humanities and Digital Sciences electives, a Tilburg minor, another Dutch university minor, or a free minor.
componentNotes.y3-capstone: Required 12-EC Sustainability Think Tank and Governance capstone linked to the selected theme; often with an external partner.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: Required 12-EC independent thesis within Interdisciplinary Social Sciences. UCR optional independent research is additional and unscheduled.
